newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives await economic news flurry.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives await economic news flurry.

text.p: The election battle over Britain's economic performance and prospects is set to intensify with the publication of a huge array of key indicators in the next 11 working days before the May 1 poll.
This week alone, Britain will publish politically-sensitive figures on job creation, public debt, earnings growth, and price inflation.
Next week will see figures for retail sales, global trade, and overall growth in the economy in the first quarter of the year.

Britain's Conservative party have made the "booming" British economy the centrepiece of their election campaign, and the raft of figures may give them extra ammunition in the run-up to polling day, economists said.

Prime Minister John Major attempted to use strong unemployment and inflation data published in March to launch his election campaign, but a flurry of allegations over sleaze distracted media and voter attention.

Since the last election in 1992, statisticians and industry pressure groups have published around 2,000 significant economic reports on the performance of the British economy, but the top indicators to be published before the election will be fresh in voters' minds.

"Many of the top economic indicators between now and polling days will be good news for the Conservatives and no doubt will be exploited to the full," said Jeremy Hawkins, economist at Bank America in London.
But he said: "They (the Conservatives) have had a wave of strong economic news over recent months and it does not seem to have made any major dent in Labour's lead in the opinion polls."
THE FOLLOWING IS A QUICK GUIDE TO THE TOP FIGURES DUE IN THE FINAL WEEKS OF THE CAMPAIGN, AND WHAT THEY ARE LIKELY TO SHOW.
* WEDNESDAY, APRIL 16

UNEMPLOYMENT figures for March forecast to show a fall in seasonally adjusted unemployment of around 47,000. Conservative leader John Major believes strong job creation -- in contrast to Britain's European partners which have more rigid economies -- is key factor in his party's favour. Unemployment fell to six year low of 6.2 percent in February. Labour will claim real level of unemployment is much higher and any new jobs are part-time and poorly paid.

AVERAGE EARNINGS data forecast to show earnings unchanged at 5.0 percent for March, a 4-1/2 year high. Although higher earnings growth makes workers feel more wealthy, a recent rise in the rate has raised inflationary concerns. Any surprise jump in the March figure, to say 5.25 percent, would spark fresh inflation concern which could overshadow the good economic news the same day from falling unemployment.

PUBLIC DEBT data -- the gap between what the government spends and collects in taxes -- has been on an improving trend as government revenues rise. Figures for March (the final month of the tax year) are forecast to show borroring requirement of 9.0 billion pounds. That would take deficit for the 1996-7 tax year to 23 billion, 3.0 billion stg lower than the latest official forecast, allowing the Conservatives to claim credit for trimming the deficit.
* THURSDAY, APRIL 17

RETAIL PRICES figures for March -- the lynchpin of government macro-economic strategy -- likely to contain good news with the core rate (exclusing home-loan costs) falling to 2.8 percent from 2.9 percent. Conservatives will argue have achieved lowest inflation rates since the 1960s but Labour will say government failed to hit its 2.5 percent inflation target by the end of the parliament. Core inflation fell below 3.0 percent in February for the first time since September.
* WEDNESDAY, APRIL 23

RETAIL SALES for March. Forecasting team at HSBC Markets provisionally estimate fairly dull figure -- flat or perhaps up slightly by around 0.2 percent on the month. Unlikely to make much political impact, though Conservatives will see as evidence consumer expenditure is moderate and no dangers of runaway boom.
* THURSDAY, APRIL 24

GLOBAL TRADE figures for February likely to show deficit of around 800 million pounds, up from 641 million pounds in January, according to HSBC Markets. Potentially politically sensitive if shows sterling strength hurting exports and pushing up trade gap, with Labour highlighting low level of industrial investment in the UK and longer-term structural trade problems.
* FRIDAY, APRIL 25

GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT data for the first quarter will be the last major politically sensitive release of the election campaign, and a key indicator of how healthy British economy really is. HSBC expect figure of around 0.8 percent, taking year-on-year rate to 2.7 percent, in line with trend growth over recent decades and a good figure for the government. But outside risk of stronger figure of 0.9 percent (annualised 3.6 percent), which could spark concern over inflation and interest rates, which might rebound on Conservatives.
